title: Ideal Body Weight Methodology
overview: Ideal body weight (IBW) formulas estimate a healthy weight range based on height and sex. These formulas were originally developed for drug dosing and clinical settings, not as strict weight goals.

methods.name: Devine Formula
methods.description: Developed by Dr. B.J. Devine in 1974 for calculating medication dosages. The most widely used IBW formula in clinical settings.

formula.name: Devine (1974)
formula.expression:
Men: IBW = 50 kg + 2.3 kg × (height in inches - 60)
Women: IBW = 45.5 kg + 2.3 kg × (height in inches - 60)

methods.accuracy: Clinical standard, but not validated for actual ideal weight
limitations: Originally for drug dosing, not weight goals
methods.author: Dr. B.J. Devine

expandedContent.history: The Devine formula was published in 1974 by Dr. B.J. Devine in the journal Drug Intelligence & Clinical Pharmacy. Unlike what many assume, Devine did not develop this formula through extensive research on ideal body weight or health outcomes. Instead, it emerged from the practical need to calculate appropriate dosages for the antibiotic gentamicin in patients with impaired renal function. Devine needed a simple way to estimate lean body mass for pharmacokinetic calculations, and his formula—based on limited data and clinical estimation—became a convenient tool. The formula's widespread adoption happened almost accidentally: it was simple, easy to memorize, and gave plausible-seeming results. Medical calculators and clinical protocols incorporated it, and within a decade it became the de facto standard for 'ideal body weight' in healthcare settings. A 2000 review by Pai and Paloucek in the Annals of Pharmacotherapy traced the formula's origins and noted that it had never been scientifically validated as a measure of true ideal weight for health purposes. Despite this, it remains embedded in clinical practice, drug dosing calculators, and ventilator settings protocols worldwide.
expandedContent.scientificBasis: The Devine formula's structure is remarkably simple: a base weight (50 kg for men, 45.5 kg for women) plus an increment of 2.3 kg per inch of height above 5 feet. This linear relationship assumes that weight should increase proportionally with height beyond a baseline threshold. The base weights correspond roughly to the expected lean body mass of a person at 5 feet tall, while the 2.3 kg/inch coefficient reflects an average rate of weight increase with height. The sex-specific base weights account for differences in bone density, muscle mass, and essential fat between men and women. However, the formula has no scientific derivation from mortality data, health outcomes, or body composition research. It was created as a clinical convenience tool and should be understood as such. The formula tends to underestimate appropriate weight for taller individuals because the linear 2.3 kg/inch relationship doesn't fully capture how body frame and muscle mass scale with increasing height. For individuals under 5 feet tall, the formula is technically undefined, though modified versions exist.
examples: A man 5'10" (70 inches): IBW = 50 + 2.3 × (70 - 60) = 50 + 23 = 73 kg (161 lbs). This gives a target for clinical calculations, not necessarily an optimal weight.
A woman 5'6" (66 inches): IBW = 45.5 + 2.3 × (66 - 60) = 45.5 + 13.8 = 59.3 kg (131 lbs). Frame size and muscle mass are not considered.
A man 6'3" (75 inches): IBW = 50 + 2.3 × (75 - 60) = 50 + 34.5 = 84.5 kg (186 lbs). For very tall individuals, this may underestimate appropriate weight.
expandedContent.comparison: The Devine formula generally produces lower ideal weight estimates than the Miller formula, especially for taller individuals. For a 6-foot tall man, Devine suggests 77.3 kg while Miller suggests 72.6 kg—both may underestimate appropriate weight for someone with a large frame or significant muscle mass. The Robinson formula produces values between Devine and Miller for most heights. The Hamwi formula tends to give higher estimates and was specifically designed for nutrition counseling rather than drug dosing. None of these formulas account for body frame size, athletic build, or ethnic differences in body composition—limitations that led to frame-size adjustments (±10%) being recommended in clinical practice.

pros: Most widely used and recognized IBW formula in clinical settings
Simple to calculate and memorize
Embedded in drug dosing protocols worldwide
Provides consistent reference point for clinical comparisons
Useful baseline for ventilator tidal volume calculations
cons: Never validated as a measure of actual ideal weight for health
Originally designed for drug dosing, not weight goals
Tends to underestimate appropriate weight for tall individuals
Does not account for frame size, muscle mass, or body composition
May promote unrealistic weight expectations if misapplied

methods.name: Robinson Formula
methods.description: Modified version of Devine's formula developed by Robinson et al. in 1983 with slightly different coefficients.

formula.name: Robinson (1983)
formula.expression:
Men: IBW = 52 kg + 1.9 kg × (height in inches - 60)
Women: IBW = 49 kg + 1.7 kg × (height in inches - 60)

methods.author: Robinson et al.

expandedContent.history: The Robinson formula was published in 1983 by J.D. Robinson and colleagues as a refinement of the Devine equation. Recognizing that the Devine formula was derived from limited data and clinical estimation rather than rigorous research, Robinson's team attempted to develop coefficients based on more systematic analysis of weight distributions in the American population. Their work drew on actuarial data from life insurance studies and Metropolitan Life Insurance Company tables, which had been tracking the relationship between weight and mortality since the 1940s. The Robinson formula uses a slightly higher base weight and a lower height coefficient than Devine, resulting in higher predicted weights at 5 feet but lower predicted weights for very tall individuals. While this represented an improvement in methodological rigor over Devine's original work, the Robinson formula still shares the fundamental limitation of attempting to define a single 'ideal' weight without accounting for individual variation in body composition, frame size, or ethnic background.
expandedContent.scientificBasis: The Robinson formula attempts to predict the weight associated with lowest mortality risk based on insurance industry data. The base weights (52 kg for men, 49 kg for women) represent estimated lean body mass at 5 feet, while the height coefficients (1.9 kg/inch for men, 1.7 kg/inch for women) reflect the average rate of weight increase with height in populations with favorable mortality outcomes. The different coefficients for men and women account for sex differences in body composition and the typical ratio of lean mass to fat mass at different heights. However, the insurance data underlying these formulas had significant limitations: it primarily represented middle-class, predominantly white Americans who could afford life insurance in the mid-20th century. Modern understanding of the relationship between weight and health recognizes that the 'ideal' weight varies considerably based on body composition, fitness level, metabolic health markers, and individual factors—nuances that simple height-based formulas cannot capture.
examples: A man 5'10" (70 inches): IBW = 52 + 1.9 × (70 - 60) = 52 + 19 = 71 kg (156 lbs)—slightly lower than Devine's 73 kg.
A woman 5'6" (66 inches): IBW = 49 + 1.7 × (66 - 60) = 49 + 10.2 = 59.2 kg (130 lbs)—nearly identical to Devine's result at this height.
A man 6'3" (75 inches): IBW = 52 + 1.9 × (75 - 60) = 52 + 28.5 = 80.5 kg (177 lbs)—4 kg lower than Devine, reflecting the flatter height coefficient.
expandedContent.comparison: Robinson produces higher values than Devine at shorter heights (due to higher base weight) but lower values at taller heights (due to lower height coefficient). At 5 feet, Robinson predicts 52 kg vs Devine's 50 kg for men. At 6'4", Robinson predicts 83.6 kg vs Devine's 89 kg. This crossover pattern means Robinson may be more appropriate for shorter individuals, while Devine (or Miller) may be more reasonable for taller people. The Miller formula, with its even higher base weight and lower coefficient, tends to produce the lowest estimates for tall individuals among the major formulas.

pros: More systematic derivation than original Devine formula
Based on actuarial mortality data
Produces more reasonable estimates for shorter individuals
Recognized alternative in clinical settings
Different height coefficients may better reflect population variation
cons: Still based on mid-20th century insurance data
Does not account for ethnic diversity in body composition
Frame size and muscle mass not considered
May underestimate appropriate weight for tall individuals
Less widely adopted than Devine in clinical protocols

methods.name: Miller Formula
methods.description: Developed by Miller et al. in 1983. Produces higher estimates than Devine for taller individuals.

formula.name: Miller (1983)
formula.expression:
Men: IBW = 56.2 kg + 1.41 kg × (height in inches - 60)
Women: IBW = 53.1 kg + 1.36 kg × (height in inches - 60)

limitations: Same fundamental limitations as other formulas
methods.author: Miller et al.

expandedContent.history: The Miller formula emerged from research published in 1983 by D.R. Miller and colleagues, developed concurrently with the Robinson formula but using different analytical approaches and data sources. Miller's team specifically aimed to address concerns that existing IBW formulas produced unrealistically low weight targets, particularly for taller individuals. Their research drew on body composition studies and anthropometric data that suggested the relationship between height and ideal weight was not as steep as earlier formulas implied. The Miller formula uses the highest base weights (56.2 kg for men, 53.1 kg for women) and the lowest height coefficients (1.41 kg/inch for men, 1.36 kg/inch for women) among the major IBW formulas. This structure produces estimates that are higher at 5 feet but converge toward (or fall below) other formulas at greater heights, reflecting the observation that very tall individuals don't necessarily need proportionally more weight per added inch of height.
expandedContent.scientificBasis: The Miller formula's structure reflects the physiological reality that the relationship between height and optimal body mass is not strictly linear. As height increases, skeletal frame dimensions increase, but the rate of increase in optimal tissue mass does not scale proportionally with each additional inch. This is because taller individuals have proportionally longer limbs but not proportionally wider torsos or greater organ mass. The high base weights in the Miller formula (56.2 kg for men, 53.1 kg for women) represent more generous estimates of lean body mass at 5 feet, while the relatively flat height coefficients (1.41 and 1.36 kg/inch) suggest that additional height contributes less to ideal weight than earlier formulas assumed. This produces a curve that rises rapidly from shorter heights but flattens as height increases—a pattern that may better reflect the actual distribution of healthy weights across the height spectrum.
examples: A man 5'10" (70 inches): IBW = 56.2 + 1.41 × (70 - 60) = 56.2 + 14.1 = 70.3 kg (155 lbs)—lower than Devine's 73 kg.
A woman 5'6" (66 inches): IBW = 53.1 + 1.36 × (66 - 60) = 53.1 + 8.16 = 61.3 kg (135 lbs)—higher than Devine's 59.3 kg.
A very tall man at 6'6" (78 inches): IBW = 56.2 + 1.41 × (78 - 60) = 56.2 + 25.4 = 81.6 kg (180 lbs)—compared to Devine's 91.4 kg, Miller is 10 kg lower.
expandedContent.comparison: The Miller formula produces the highest estimates for shorter individuals and the lowest estimates for very tall individuals among the major IBW formulas. At 5 feet, Miller's 56.2 kg (men) exceeds Devine's 50 kg and Robinson's 52 kg. However, by 6'6", Miller's 81.6 kg falls well below Devine's 91.4 kg. This crossover pattern makes Miller potentially more appropriate for shorter people who might find Devine's targets unrealistically low, but it may underestimate appropriate weight for very tall individuals with substantial frames. The Hamwi formula, designed for nutrition counseling, typically produces the highest estimates across the height range.

pros: Produces more realistic targets for shorter individuals
Based on body composition research
Reflects non-linear relationship between height and weight
May reduce unrealistic expectations for shorter people
Alternative perspective when other formulas seem too aggressive
cons: May underestimate appropriate weight for very tall individuals
Less widely used in clinical settings than Devine
Limited validation compared to other formulas
Still does not account for frame size or body composition
May seem inconsistent with other IBW estimates

methods.name: Hamwi Formula
methods.description: Developed by Dr. G.J. Hamwi in 1964 for dietetic purposes. Popular in nutrition counseling.

formula.name: Hamwi (1964)
formula.expression:
Men: IBW = 48 kg + 2.7 kg × (height in inches - 60)
Women: IBW = 45.5 kg + 2.2 kg × (height in inches - 60)

limitations: Developed before modern research on body composition
methods.author: Dr. G.J. Hamwi

expandedContent.history: The Hamwi formula was developed by Dr. George J. Hamwi, an endocrinologist at Ohio State University, and first appeared in the 1964 American Diabetes Association publication 'Changing Dietary Concepts.' Hamwi created this formula specifically for nutrition counseling and dietary planning rather than drug dosing—a fundamentally different purpose than the later Devine formula. His goal was to provide dietitians with a simple tool for establishing caloric needs and weight goals for patients, particularly those with diabetes who needed careful dietary management. The formula predates the other major IBW equations and was designed with a more generous approach to weight estimation, reflecting mid-20th century nutritional thinking that favored somewhat higher weights than later clinical formulas would suggest. Hamwi also introduced the concept of adjusting for frame size by adding or subtracting 10% for large or small frames, an adjustment that remains commonly recommended alongside all IBW formulas.
expandedContent.scientificBasis: The Hamwi formula's structure uses a lower base weight (48 kg for men, 45.5 kg for women) but a steeper height coefficient (2.7 kg/inch for men, 2.2 kg/inch for women) compared to most alternatives. This combination produces relatively moderate weights at shorter heights but higher weights for taller individuals. The steeper coefficient reflects Hamwi's clinical observation that taller patients often needed more calories and could maintain health at weights that might seem high by strict actuarial standards. The formula was developed before extensive research on obesity and mortality refined our understanding of the weight-health relationship. Hamwi's original recommendation included frame size adjustments: subtracting 10% for small frames and adding 10% for large frames, based on elbow breadth or wrist circumference measurements. This acknowledgment of individual variation represented an advance over simple height-only formulas, even though the basic equation itself remains limited.
examples: A man 5'10" (70 inches): IBW = 48 + 2.7 × (70 - 60) = 48 + 27 = 75 kg (165 lbs)—higher than Devine's 73 kg.
A woman 5'6" (66 inches): IBW = 45.5 + 2.2 × (66 - 60) = 45.5 + 13.2 = 58.7 kg (129 lbs)—similar to other formulas at this height.
A large-framed man 6'2" (74 inches): Base IBW = 48 + 2.7 × (74 - 60) = 48 + 37.8 = 85.8 kg. With +10% frame adjustment: 94.4 kg (208 lbs).
expandedContent.comparison: Hamwi generally produces the highest IBW estimates for tall individuals due to its steep height coefficient. For someone 6 feet tall, Hamwi suggests 81 kg vs Devine's 77 kg—a meaningful 4 kg difference. At shorter heights, the lower base weight brings Hamwi closer to other formulas. The formula's origins in nutrition counseling rather than drug dosing make it arguably more appropriate for setting dietary goals, though it shares the fundamental limitations of all IBW formulas in not accounting for body composition. When combined with frame size adjustments, Hamwi can produce a reasonable range of target weights rather than a single point estimate.

pros: Designed specifically for nutrition counseling purposes
Includes original recommendation for frame size adjustment
Predates the drug-dosing origins of other formulas
Produces more generous estimates for tall individuals
Widely used in dietetics education and practice
cons: Developed before modern body composition research
May overestimate appropriate weight for some individuals
Frame size adjustments are subjective
Less validated than Devine for clinical calculations
Older formula may not reflect current understanding of healthy weight

footnotes: All formulas assume medium body frame
Frame size adjustment: ±10% for small/large frames
Modern approach: focus on body composition, not just weight
disclaimer: Ideal weight formulas provide rough estimates. Healthy weight depends on many factors including muscle mass, bone density, and overall health. Consult a healthcare provider for personalized guidance.
